card.name: Chholiya
card.tagline: A thousand-year-old Himalayan martial sword dance guarding marriage processions.
card.profile: Chholiya is a traditional martial sword dance native to the Kumaon division of Uttarakhand, India, and the Sudurpashchim province of Nepal. Performed by troupes of twenty-two men—eight sword dancers and fourteen musicians—the form originated over a thousand years ago among warring Kshatriya clans. Clad in warrior cholas, white churidar payajamas, and sandalwood face paste, the dancers engage in synchronized mock duels to the sound of brass horns, bagpipes, and native drums. While fundamentally an apotropaic ritual designed to protect wedding processions from malevolent spirits, it is now presented across many auspicious gatherings.
card.insight: Dating to 10th-century Kumaon wars when marriages were won at sword-point, 22-man troupes brandish tulwars and brass shields to ward off demons trailing the groom.

card.profile_long:
Chholiya stands as a living testament to the medieval martial traditions of the Central Himalayas, originating more than a thousand years ago in the rugged terrain of the Kumaon division of Uttarakhand, India, and neighbouring Sudurpashchim province in Nepal. Its historical roots stem directly from the warring Kshatriya clans—specifically the native Khasas, Katyuris, and immigrant Rajputs who were consolidated under the rule of the Chand Kings in the 10th century. During this ancient era, marriages among rival Kshatriyas were frequently conducted at the point of the sword. Although forceful bridal abduction subsided as political authority centralized, the fierce ceremonial customs survived: to this day, the groom in Kumaon is revered as 'Kunwar' or 'Raja' (king), rides on horseback, and carries a khukuri in his belt, accompanied by sword-wielding dancers who preserve the battlefield rites of his ancestors.

Beyond its martial demonstration, Chholiya serves an essential apotropaic and spiritual purpose within Himalayan society. Traditionally executed primarily by Rajput men leading the wedding party (baryat or barat), the dance is considered deeply auspicious because of its protective power against hostile spirits and demons. Popular belief held that weddings were vulnerable occasions where malicious entities stalked processions to steal away the couple's good fortune and bewitch the newlyweds. The clash of blades, the waving of banners, and the thunderous sonic barrier raised by accompanying musicians were deemed potent enough to disperse these invisible forces and ensure safe passage for the groom's entourage.

A complete Chholiya contingent constitutes a tightly coordinated team of twenty-two men: eight dedicated sword dancers and fourteen instrumentalists. The dancers perform synchronized steps, weaving through deliberate spatial formations while engaging their partners in fierce mock combats. Brandishing curved tulwar swords in one hand and sturdy brass shields in the other, they elevate their weapons and charge with focused, intense facial expressions designed to project the fierce temperament of warriors entering mortal combat. At the vanguard of the unit, performers carry the 'nishana', a vibrant triangular red flag that signals the arrival of the troop and rallies the procession.

The music propelling Chholiya is combative and resonant, rooted in brass and percussion instruments once used on battlefields to elevate troop morale. Ancient curved brass horns, such as the turi, the serpentine nagphani, and the ransing, blast piercing fanfares over the heavy, syncopated rhythms of the dhol barrel drum and damau kettle drum, operated by hereditary professional musicians known as dholies. In addition to native woodwinds like the nine-note nausuriya muruli and the double-flute jyonya, the music features the masakbeen—a Scottish highland bagpipe assimilated into Kumaoni culture during the British colonial period—which creates the unmistakable wailing drone central to Pahari celebrations today.

The dancers' visual presentation reflects ancient battlefield regalia. Performers wear a flowing warrior gown known as the chola over a white churidar payajama, secure their heads with the traditional taanka, and coat their faces in pale sandalwood paste, evoking warriors prepared for combat. Throughout Kumaon, Chholiya has diversified into distinct sub-traditions, including Bisu nritya, the mock combat of Saranv, Rann Nritya ('war dance'), Sarankar, Veerangna, Depanshu, the distinct regional Shauka Shaili of the Johar region, Chholiya Baja, and Paitan Baja, anchoring Himalayan communal celebration in martial history.

card.sacred_note: Chholiya carries an apotropaic religious function: performed during wedding processions (barat/baryat), it is believed to actively protect the couple by warding off malevolent spirits and demons attracted to human happiness. Outsiders should respect its ceremonial protective role during marriage rituals.

sections.origins_and_history: Chholiya traces its lineage back more than a thousand years to the warring Kshatriya clans of the Kumaon hills, including the Katyuris and Khasas, during an era when alliances and marriages were sealed at the point of the sword. When the Chand Dynasty rose in the 10th century, arriving Rajput lineages merged with local communities and adopted Pahari language and customs, establishing a lasting martial ethos. Although the era of sword-point marriage raids ended, its theatrical and ceremonial residue persisted: the groom retains the title of Kunwar or King, travels on horseback, and wears a khukuri in his belt, preceded by martial escorts.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by an ensemble of twenty-two men, composed of eight sword dancers and fourteen musicians. The eight dancers move in synchronized alignments, alternating between collective marching steps and paired mock combats (saraanv). Clasping curved tulwar swords and brass shields, dancers advance with the nishana—a triangular red banner—held high, assuming fierce battlefield expressions while clashing their weapons together. Specific footwork counts, meters, and basic technical drills are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical accompaniment is provided by fourteen musicians playing traditional martial and regional instruments. Percussion is driven by the dhol and damau, played by hereditary musicians called dholies. Brass war horns include the curved turi, the snake-shaped nagphani, and the ransing. The ensemble also uses native woodwinds—the nausuriya muruli (nine-note flute) and the jyonya (twin flute)—alongside the masakbeen (Scottish bagpipe), which was assimilated into the Kumaoni brass and pipe tradition from British marching bands.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear traditional Kumaoni warrior attire consisting of a chola over white churidar payajama, topped with a taanka headpiece. Their faces are smeared with sandalwood paste, mirroring warriors sanctifying themselves for war. Each dancer carries a steel tulwar sword and a round brass shield, accompanied by the nishana, a triangular red flag. The dance is performed outdoors, traversing mountain paths during wedding processions (baryat/barat) or standing before auspicious communal celebrations.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: While rooted in martial pageantry, Chholiya possesses significant religious and apotropaic weight, particularly among Rajput communities. Wedding processions were traditionally believed to be open targets for demons and malevolent spirits seeking to ruin human happiness. By waving swords, engaging in mock battles, and sounding martial horns, Chholiya dancers actively purify the procession path, warding off demonic forces to protect the bride and groom.
sections.notable_figures: The sources mention historical groups rather than individual performers: the Chand Kings of the 10th century, the Katyuri kings, the Khasas, and the Rajput lineages who shaped Pahari culture, alongside hereditary dholie drummers who maintain the musical lineages.
sections.regional_variants: The dance exists across multiple named regional and stylistic forms: Bisu nritya, Saranv (focused on mock duels), Rann Nritya ('war dance'), Sarankar, Veerangna, Depanshu, Chholiya Baja, Paitan Baja, and Shauka Shaili, which is native to the Johar region of Kumaon.
sections.lineage: Historically passed through Rajput and Khas communities of the Central Himalayas alongside hereditary dholie percussionist castes. Originating in medieval Kumaon and western Nepal, the form has spread across Almora, Bageshwar, Champawat, Pithoragarh, Doti, Baitadi, Darchula, the Garhwal division, and Khas communities in Sikkim.

claims.text: Chholiya is a traditional folk sword dance originating in the Kumaon division of Uttarakhand, India, and Sudurpashchim province of Nepal.
The dance has a history stretching back over a millennium to Kumaon's martial traditions.
A full team of performers consists of twenty-two men, divided into eight dancers and fourteen musicians.
The dance was historically performed during weddings to protect the procession from demons and evil spirits.
Dancers wear a chola, white churidar payajama, head taanka, and sandalwood paste on their faces while bearing tulwars and brass shields.
The musical ensemble incorporates traditional brass war horns, drums played by dholies, native woodwinds, and the British-introduced masakbeen bagpipe.
The groom rides a horse in the wedding procession and wears a khukuri knife in his belt, reflecting historical royal titles.
Chholiya is practiced today as a living tradition in Indian and Nepalese Himalayan districts.

music_profile.sound_description: A booming, warlike outdoor soundscape defined by the thunderous pairing of dhol and damau drums played by dholies, punctured by the piercing brass calls of the turi, ransing, and serpentine nagphani. Over this martial percussion, the wailing reed drone of the masakbeen bagpipe intertwines with high woodwind melodies of the nausuriya muruli and twin flutes.

episode_brief.logline: High in the Himalayas of Kumaon and Nepal, twenty-two men sound war horns and clash tulwar swords to protect a bridegroom from demonic ambush.
beats: A wedding party moves along an Almora mountain trail; the groom sits mounted on a horse wearing a khukuri in his sash.
The 14-man orchestra unleashes the roar of the dhol, damau, and the piercing bray of the ransing and masakbeen.
Eight dancers step forward, faces covered in white sandalwood paste, brandishing the triangular red nishana banner.
The troupe splits into paired mock duels (saraanv), clashing curved tulwars against brass shields to deflect demons.
Elder community members recount how 10th-century Chand kings unified Rajput and Katyuri clans when brides were won at sword point.
The procession arrives safely at the wedding grounds, the protective cordon completed under mountain skies.
